claim: BigBrain is a singular 3D volumetric reconstruction of a sliced and cell-body stained post mortem human brain.
source: BigBrain is a singular 3D volumetric reconstruction of a sliced and cell-body stained post mortem human brain (Amunts et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Amunts et al., 2013.

claim: BigBrain allows computational analysis of the entire organ in relation to cell staining at resolutions up to 20 µm.
source: This resource allows computational analysis of the entire organ in relation to cell staining at high resolutions (up to 20 µm).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing BigBrain's capabilities.

claim: BigBrain is made available in common MRI formats (minc and NifTI).
source: It is specially tailored for neuroimagers, as it is made available in common MRI formats (minc and NifTI), accompanied by cortical surface reconstructions (Lewis et al., 2014), and nonlinearly registered to standard MRI templates (ICBM152 and MNI-ADNI) (Fonov et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing BigBrain's format availability.

claim: BigBrain is accompanied by cortical surface reconstructions.
source: It is specially tailored for neuroimagers, as it is made available in common MRI formats (minc and NifTI), accompanied by cortical surface reconstructions (Lewis et al., 2014), and nonlinearly registered to standard MRI templates (ICBM152 and MNI-ADNI) (Fonov et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Lewis et al., 2014.

claim: BigBrain is nonlinearly registered to standard MRI templates (ICBM152 and MNI-ADNI).
source: It is specially tailored for neuroimagers, as it is made available in common MRI formats (minc and NifTI), accompanied by cortical surface reconstructions (Lewis et al., 2014), and nonlinearly registered to standard MRI templates (ICBM152 and MNI-ADNI) (Fonov et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Fonov et al., 2011a.

claim: Recent studies have expanded BigBrain by offering improved registrations to standard spaces.
source: Furthermore, recent studies have expanded the resource by offering improved registrations to standard spaces (Lewis et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2019), nuanced intracortical surface models, and laminar approximations (Wagstyl et al., 2018a; Wagstyl et al., 2020) as well as regional segmentations (DeKraker et al., 2019; Xiao et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2020 and Xiao et al., 2019.

claim: Recent studies have expanded BigBrain by offering nuanced intracortical surface models and laminar approximations.
source: Furthermore, recent studies have expanded the resource by offering improved registrations to standard spaces (Lewis et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2019), nuanced intracortical surface models, and laminar approximations (Wagstyl et al., 2018a; Wagstyl et al., 2020) as well as regional segmentations (DeKraker et al., 2019; Xiao et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Wagstyl et al., 2018a and Wagstyl et al., 2020.

claim: Recent studies have expanded BigBrain by offering regional segmentations.
source: Furthermore, recent studies have expanded the resource by offering improved registrations to standard spaces (Lewis et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2019), nuanced intracortical surface models, and laminar approximations (Wagstyl et al., 2018a; Wagstyl et al., 2020) as well as regional segmentations (DeKraker et al., 2019; Xiao et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to DeKraker et al., 2019 and Xiao et al., 2019.

claim: Several studies have capitalised on BigBrain for integrative histological-neuroimaging analyses, including comparison of cytoarchitectural and functional gradients.
source: Several studies have already capitalised on this unique resource for integrative histological-neuroimaging analyses, including comparison of cytoarchitectural and functional gradients (Paquola et al., 2019), cross-validation of in vivo defined microstructural gradients in the insula with histological measures (Royer et al., 2020), mapping variations in functional connectivity along the histological axis of the mesiotemporal lobe (Paquola et al., 2020b), fMRI responses of the histologically defined auditory system (Sitek et al., 2019), comparison of cytoarchitectural similarity with MRI-derived estimates of structural connectivity (Wei et al., 2019), and analysis of the cytoarchitectural similarity of large-scale network hubs (Arnatkevičiute et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Paquola et al., 2019.

claim: The reconstruction of BigBrain involved coronal slicing of a complete paraffin-embedded brain (65-year-old male) into 7404 sections at 20 μm thickness.
source: In brief, the reconstruction of BigBrain involved coronal slicing of a complete paraffin-embedded brain (65-year-old male) into 7404 sections at 20 μm thickness.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the BigBrain reconstruction process.

claim: Each section of BigBrain was stained for cell bodies using Merker staining.
source: Each section was stained for cell bodies (Merker, 1983), digitised, and subjected to manual and automatic artefact repair.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Merker, 1983.

claim: The volumetric reconstruction of BigBrain is available online at 40 µm, 100 µm, 200 µm, 300 µm, 400 µm, and 1000 µm resolutions.
source: The volumetric reconstruction is available online at 40 µm, 100 µm, 200 µm, 300 µm, 400 µm, and 1000 µm resolutions (http://bigbrainproject.org).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the available resolutions of BigBrain.

claim: The 40 µm version of BigBrain is released as 125 individual blocks corresponding to five subdivisions in the x, y, and z directions, with overlap.
source: The 40 µm version is released as 125 individual blocks corresponding to five subdivisions in the x, y, and z directions, with overlap.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the structure of the 40 µm version.

claim: Merker staining labels cell bodies, similar to Nissl staining, with a high contrast between black cell bodies on a light background.
source: The Merker staining labels cell bodies, similar to Nissl staining, with a high contrast between black cell bodies on a light background (Merker, 1983).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Merker, 1983.

claim: The grey and white matter boundaries of the cortical surface released in 2014 contain 163,842 vertices on each hemisphere.
source: The grey and white matter boundaries of the cortical surface released in 2014 contain 163,842 vertices on each hemisphere, with vertices aligned between pial and white surfaces (Lewis et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Lewis et al., 2014.

claim: Surfaces of BigBrain were generated using a modified version of CIVET.
source: Surfaces were generated using a modified version of CIVET (Kim et al., 2005; MacDonald et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Kim et al., 2005 and MacDonald et al., 2000.

claim: Sampling staining intensity from many cortical depths provides a profile of the cytoarchitecture.
source: Sampling staining intensity from many cortical depths provides a profile of the cytoarchitecture, hereafter referred to as a staining intensity profile.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the method for obtaining staining intensity profiles.

claim: The current approach for sampling staining intensity involves equivolumetric surface construction.
source: The current approach involves equivolumetric surface construction, whereby a set of intracortical surfaces are initialised at equidistant depths, then modulated by cortical curvature (Waehnert et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Waehnert et al., 2014.

claim: Equivolumetric surface construction holds advantages for histological data because laminae vary in thickness depending on cortical folding.
source: This holds advantages for histological data because laminae vary in thickness depending on cortical folding (Bok, 1929).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Bok, 1929.

claim: Smoothing can be employed in tangential and axial directions to ameliorate the effects of artefacts, blood vessels, and individual neuronal arrangement.
source: Smoothing can be employed in tangential and axial directions to ameliorate the effects of artefacts, blood vessels, and individual neuronal arrangement (Wagstyl et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Wagstyl et al., 2018a.

claim: For the initial BigBrainWarp release, 50 surfaces, 2 iterations of depth-wise smoothing and 2 FWHM surface-wise smoothing were selected.
source: For the initial BigBrainWarp release, we selected 50 surfaces, 2 iterations of depth-wise smoothing and (a modest) 2 FWHM surface-wise smoothing.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the parameters chosen for BigBrainWarp.

claim: The isocortex contains six layers.
source: The isocortex contains six layers (Brodmann, 1909), certain features of which manifest on BigBrain staining intensity profiles.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Brodmann, 1909.

claim: The transition from layer I to II exhibits a sharp increase in staining because layer I is only sparsely populated with cells, while the outer granular layer II has a higher density.
source: The transition from layer I to II exhibits a sharp increase in staining because layer I is only sparsely populated with cells, while the outer granular layer II has a higher density.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing features of staining intensity profiles.

claim: Layer IV harbours a second, noticeable peak in cell staining, corresponding to dense packing of granule cells.
source: Layer IV harbours a second, noticeable peak in cell staining, corresponding to dense packing of granule cells.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing features of staining intensity profiles.

claim: The peak of layer IV corresponds to the division between supragranular and infragranular layers, which have markedly different roles in neural communication.
source: The peak of layer IV corresponds to the division between supragranular and infragranular layers, which have markedly different roles in neural communication (Buffalo et al., 2011; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Rockland and Pandya, 1979).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Buffalo et al., 2011, Felleman and Van Essen, 1991, and Rockland and Pandya, 1979.

claim: The relative depth of layer IV is potentially informative, likely related to the propensity for feedforward vs feedback communication.
source: The relative depth of layer IV is also potentially informative, likely related to the propensity for feedforward vs feedback communication (Beul et al., 2017; Sanides, 1962; Wagstyl et al., 2018a), though the demarcation of feedforward and feedback projections is more multifactorial and complex (Rockland, 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Beul et al., 2017, Sanides, 1962, Wagstyl et al., 2018a, and Rockland, 2015.

claim: A six-layered decomposition of the BigBrain isocortex has been produced by training a convolutional neural network on manual annotations in 51 regions.
source: A six-layered decomposition of the BigBrain isocortex has also been produced by training a convolutional neural network on manual annotations in 51 regions, then extending the model to the whole isocortex (Wagstyl et al., 2020; Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Wagstyl et al., 2020, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Laminar thickness estimates aligned with prior histological studies while increasing overall spatial precision.
source: Laminar thickness estimates aligned with prior histological studies (Von Economo and Koskinas, 1925), while increasing overall spatial precision.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Von Economo and Koskinas, 1925.

claim: Moment-based parameterisation of staining intensity profiles involves calculating the central moments of each staining intensity profile and the derivative profile.
source: This technique, pioneered by the Jülich group (Schleicher et al., 1999; Zilles et al., 2002), involves calculating the central moments (i.e., mean, the center of gravity, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis) of each staining intensity profile and the derivative profile, resulting in a multidimensional feature vector for each cortical point.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Schleicher et al., 1999 and Zilles et al., 2002.

claim: The mean of staining intensity profiles has been related to overall cellular density.
source: For example, the mean has been related to overall cellular density (Wree et al., 1982).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Wree et al., 1982.

claim: Skewness of staining intensity profiles varies from sensory to limbic areas and indexes the balance of cellular density in infra- vs supra-granular layers.
source: In contrast, skewness varies from sensory to limbic areas (i.e., sensory-fugal) and indexes the balance of cellular density in infra- vs supra-granular layers (Paquola et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Paquola et al., 2020b.

claim: Observer-independent discrimination of cortical areas can be accomplished by comparing moment-based feature vectors between neighbouring vertices.
source: Observer-independent discrimination of cortical areas can be accomplished by comparing moment-based feature vectors between neighbouring vertices (Schleicher et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Schleicher et al., 1999.

claim: Over the past 20 years, moment-based feature vector comparison has been employed in 23 post mortem brains, including BigBrain, resulting in a 3D probabilistic atlas of the human brain.
source: Over the past 20 years, this procedure has been employed in 23 post mortem brains, including BigBrain, resulting in a 3D probabilistic atlas of the human brain (Amunts et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Amunts et al., 2020.

claim: Cortex-wide cytoarchitectural similarity may be estimated by cross-correlating staining intensity profiles between different cortical locations.
source: Cortex-wide cytoarchitectural similarity may also be estimated by cross-correlating staining intensity profiles between different cortical locations (Paquola et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Paquola et al., 2019.

claim: Diffusion map embedding was applied to the profile cross-correlation matrix of BigBrain to identify principle axes of cytoarchitectural differentiation.
source: We recently applied diffusion map embedding, a nonlinear manifold learning technique (Coifman and Lafon, 2006), to the profile cross-correlation matrix of BigBrain to identify principle axes of cytoarchitectural differentiation (Paquola et al., 2019; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Coifman and Lafon, 2006 and Paquola et al., 2019, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The first two eigenvectors of cytoarchitectural gradients explain approximately 42% and 35% of variance, respectively.
source: Here, the first two eigenvectors explain approximately 42% and 35% of variance, respectively, and describe anterior–posterior and sensory-fugal axes (further details in Tutorial 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the results of the analysis.

claim: The first two eigenvectors of cytoarchitectural gradients describe anterior–posterior and sensory-fugal axes.
source: Here, the first two eigenvectors explain approximately 42% and 35% of variance, respectively, and describe anterior–posterior and sensory-fugal axes (further details in Tutorial 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the results of the analysis.

claim: Manual segmentations of the putamen, caudate nucleus, globus pallidus pars externa, globus pallidus pars interna, nucleus accumbens, amygdala, thalamus, red nucleus, substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus, and the hippocampus are available on Open Science Framework.
source: Manual segmentations of the putamen, caudate nucleus, globus pallidus pars externa, globus pallidus pars interna, nucleus accumbens, amygdala, thalamus, red nucleus, substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus, and the hippocampus are available on Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/xkqb3/).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing available resources.

claim: A recent study used anatomical landmarks to create an internal coordinate system of the hippocampus by solving Laplace's equation under three sets of boundary conditions: anterior–posterior, proximal–distal, and inner–outer.
source: Extending upon whole-structure segmentation, a recent study DeKraker et al., 2019 used anatomical landmarks to create an internal coordinate system of the hippocampus. The approach involved solving Laplace's equation under three sets of boundary conditions: anterior–posterior, proximal–distal (relative to the subiculum), and inner–outer (DeKraker et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to DeKraker et al., 2019 and DeKraker et al., 2018.

claim: The hippocampus can be 'unfolded' using the internal coordinate system, allowing examination of histological and morphometric features in a topologically continuous space.
source: Subsequently, the hippocampus can be 'unfolded', allowing examination of histological and morphometric features in a topologically continuous space (Figure 1F), in line with other surface-based studies of the hippocampus (Bernhardt et al., 2016; Caldairou et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2014; Vos de Wael et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations, with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: The 3D coordinate system of the hippocampus enabled the creation of a continuous surface model of the mesiotemporal cortex.
source: Furthermore, this 3D coordinate system enabled the creation of a continuous surface model of the mesiotemporal cortex (Paquola et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Paquola et al., 2020b.

claim: Registration of BigBrain to MRI templates involves additional challenges, including histological artefacts, differences in intensity contrasts and inter-individual variability.
source: Registration of BigBrain to MRI templates involves additional challenges, however, including histological artefacts, differences in intensity contrasts and inter-individual variability.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing challenges in BigBrain-MRI registration.

claim: For the initial BigBrain release, full BigBrain volumes were resampled to ICBM2009sym and MNI-ADNI.
source: For the initial BigBrain release (Amunts et al., 2013), full BigBrain volumes were resampled to ICBM2009sym (a symmetric MNI152 template) and MNI-ADNI (an older adult T1-weighted template) (Fonov et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Amunts et al., 2013 and Fonov et al., 2011a.

claim: Registration of BigBrain to ICBM2009sym involved a linear then a nonlinear transformation.
source: Registration of BigBrain to ICBM2009sym, known as BigBrainSym, involved a linear then a nonlinear transformation (available on ftp://bigbrain.loris.ca/BigBrainRelease.2015/).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the registration process.

claim: The nonlinear transformation for BigBrainSym was defined by a symmetric diffeomorphic optimiser (SyN algorithm) that maximised the cross-correlation of the BigBrain volume with inverted intensities and a population-averaged T1-weighted map in ICBM2009sym space.
source: The nonlinear transformation was defined by a symmetric diffeomorphic optimiser (SyN algorithm; Avants et al., 2008) that maximised the cross-correlation of the BigBrain volume with inverted intensities and a population-averaged T1-weighted map in ICBM2009sym space.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Avants et al., 2008.

claim: A prior study improved the accuracy of the transformation for subcortical structures and the hippocampus using a two-stage multi-contrast registration.
source: A prior study (Xiao et al., 2019) was able to further improve the accuracy of the transformation for subcortical structures and the hippocampus using a two-stage multi-contrast registration.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Xiao et al., 2019.

claim: The first stage of the two-stage multi-contrast registration involved nonlinear registration of BigBrainSym to a PD25 T1-T2* fusion atlas, using manual segmentations as additional shape priors.
source: The first stage involved nonlinear registration of BigBrainSym to a PD25 T1-T2* fusion atlas (Xiao et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2015), using manual segmentations of the basal ganglia, red nucleus, thalamus, amygdala, and hippocampus as additional shape priors.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Xiao et al., 2017 and Xiao et al., 2015.

claim: The PD25 T1-T2* fusion contrast is more similar to the BigBrainSym intensity contrast than a T1-weighted image.
source: Notably, the PD25 T1-T2* fusion contrast is more similar to the BigBrainSym intensity contrast than a T1-weighted image.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the registration approach.

claim: The two-stage procedure resulted in 0.86–0.97 DICE coefficients for region labels, improving upon direct overlap of BigBrainSym with ICBM2009sym (0.55–0.91 DICE).
source: The two-stage procedure resulted in 0.86–0.97 DICE coefficients for region labels, improving upon direct overlap of BigBrainSym with ICBM2009sym (0.55–0.91 DICE) (Figure 2Aii,Aiv, top).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2Aii,Aiv.

claim: Transformed anatomical fiducials exhibited 1.77 ± 1.25 mm errors, on par with direct overlap of BigBrainSym with ICBM2009sym (1.83 ± 1.47 mm).
source: Transformed anatomical fiducials exhibited 1.77 ± 1.25 mm errors, on par with direct overlap of BigBrainSym with ICBM2009sym (1.83 ± 1.47 mm) (Figure 2Aiii,Aiv, below).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2Aiii,Aiv.

claim: The unique morphology of BigBrain presents challenges for surface-based transformations, especially in the anterior cingulate.
source: The unique morphology of BigBrain also presents challenges for surface-based transformations. Idiosyncratic gyrification of certain regions of BigBrain, especially the anterior cingulate, cause misregistration (Lewis et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Lewis et al., 2020.

claim: The areal midline representation of BigBrain, following inflation to a sphere, is disproportionately smaller than standard surface templates.
source: Additionally, the areal midline representation of BigBrain, following inflation to a sphere, is disproportionately smaller than standard surface templates, which is related to differences in surface area, in hemisphere separation methods, and in tessellation methods.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing challenges in surface-based transformations.

claim: Ongoing work combines a specialised BigBrain surface mesh with multimodal surface matching (MSM) to co-register BigBrain to standard surface templates.
source: To overcome these issues, ongoing work (Lewis et al., 2020) combines a specialised BigBrain surface mesh with multimodal surface matching (MSM; Robinson et al., 2018; Robinson et al., 2014) to co-register BigBrain to standard surface templates.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2020, Robinson et al., 2018, and Robinson et al., 2014.

claim: BigBrain surface meshes were re-tessellated as unstructured meshes with variable vertex density to be more compatible with FreeSurfer generated meshes.
source: In the first step, the BigBrain surface meshes were re-tessellated as unstructured meshes with variable vertex density (Möbius and Kobbelt, 2010) to be more compatible with FreeSurfer generated meshes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Möbius and Kobbelt, 2010.

claim: Coarse-to-fine MSM registration was applied in three stages: affine rotation, nonlinear/discrete alignment using sulcal depth maps, and nonlinear/discrete alignment using curvature maps.
source: Then, coarse-to-fine MSM registration was applied in three stages. An affine rotation was applied to the BigBrain sphere, with an additional 'nudge' based on an anterior cingulate landmark. Next, nonlinear/discrete alignment using sulcal depth maps (emphasising global scale, Figure 2Biii), followed by nonlinear/discrete alignment using curvature maps (emphasising finer detail, Figure 2Biii).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2Biii.

claim: The modified MSMsulc+curv pipeline improves the accuracy of transformed cortical maps (4.38 ± 3.25 mm), compared to a standard MSMsulc approach (8.02 ± 7.53 mm).
source: This modified MSMsulc+curv pipeline improves the accuracy of transformed cortical maps (4.38 ± 3.25 mm), compared to a standard MSMsulc approach (8.02 ± 7.53 mm) (Figure 2Bii–iii; Lewis et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2Bii–iii and a citation to Lewis et al., 2020.

claim: BigBrainWarp is a modular set of scripts that maps between common BigBrain and MRI spaces.
source: For BigBrainWarp, a modular set of scripts maps between common BigBrain and MRI spaces.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing BigBrainWarp.

claim: The bigbrainwarp function allows input and output of data that is aligned to the BigBrain volume, BigBrainSym volume, ICBM152 2009b symmetric volume, BigBrain surface, fsaverage or fs_LR.
source: The bigbrainwarp function allows input and output of data that is aligned to the BigBrain volume, BigBrainSym volume, ICBM152 2009b symmetric volume, BigBrain surface (synonymous with BigBrainSym surface), fsaverage or fs_LR (164 k and 32 k versions).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the functionality of bigbrainwarp.

claim: Containerisation of BigBrainWarp via Docker allows users to interact with the scripts without installing dependencies.
source: Furthermore, containerisation of BigBrainWarp via Docker allows users to interact with the scripts without installing dependencies.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing BigBrainWarp's containerisation.

claim: BigBrainWarp was used to map histological gradients to fsaverage, fs_LR and ICBM152.
source: We used BigBrainWarp to map histological gradients, discussed above, to fsaverage, fs_LR and ICBM152.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the use of BigBrainWarp.

claim: BigBrainWarp was used to transform in vivo derived microstructural and functional gradients, as well as intrinsic functional communities, to the BigBrain surface.
source: Conversely, we used BigBrainWarp to transform in vivo derived microstructural and functional gradients, as well as intrinsic functional communities (Yeo et al., 2011), to the BigBrain surface.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Yeo et al., 2011.

claim: For the initial release of BigBrainWarp, the multi-scale imaging connectomics (MICs) dataset was selected, which contains group-level features on standard surface templates from 50 healthy adults.
source: For the initial release of BigBrainWarp, we selected the multi-scale imaging connectomics (MICs) dataset, which contains group-level features on standard surface templates from 50 healthy adults (Royer et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Royer et al., 2021.

claim: Tutorial 1 demonstrates how BigBrain can be used to initialise region of interest analyses, such as mapping resting-state functional connectivity along the iso-to-allocortical axis.
source: In tutorial 1, we show how BigBrain can be used to initialise region of interest analyses, such as mapping resting-state functional connectivity along the iso-to-allocortical axis (Paquola et al., 2020b), enabling delineation of regions that are difficult to identify with in vivo imaging and functional interrogation of histological axes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Paquola et al., 2020b.

claim: Tutorial 2 demonstrates how cytoarchitectural gradients can help to characterise large-scale cortical patterns, such as the association of aging with Aβ deposition.
source: In tutorial 2, we show how cytoarchitectural gradients can help to characterise large-scale cortical patterns, such as the association of aging with Aβ deposition (Lowe et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Lowe et al., 2019.

claim: Tutorial 3 discusses moment-based parameterisation of staining intensity profiles to evaluate homogeneity within imaging-based parcellations.
source: In tutorial 3, we discuss more specific histological features, namely moment-based parameterisation of staining intensity profiles (Schleicher et al., 1999; Zilles et al., 2002). These features depict the vast cytoarchitectural heterogeneity of the cortex and enable evaluation of homogeneity within imaging-based parcellations, for example macroscale functional communities (Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Schleicher et al., 1999, Zilles et al., 2002, and Yeo et al., 2011.

claim: The optimal model for predicting regional variation in effect of age on Aβ deposition included only Hist-G2, indicating that Aβ preferentially accumulates towards the more agranular anchor of the sensory-fugal gradient.
source: The optimal model included only Hist-G2, indicating that Aβ preferentially accumulates towards the more agranular anchor of the sensory-fugal gradient.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the results of Tutorial 2.

claim: Visual networks have the highest mean and lowest skewness of staining intensity profiles.
source: For example, the mean and skewness illustrate distinct patterns of cytoarchitectural differentiation across the functional networks. Visual networks have the highest mean and lowest skewness.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the results of Tutorial 3.

claim: Ventral attention, limbic, and fronto-parietal networks harbour the lowest mean and highest skewness of staining intensity profiles.
source: Ventral attention, limbic, and fronto-parietal networks harbour the lowest mean and highest skewness, whereas the default mode networks occupy an intermediary position.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the results of Tutorial 3.

claim: Visual networks harbour distinctive cytoarchitecture, reflected by relatively high accuracy and few incorrect predictions in classification.
source: Visual networks harbour distinctive cytoarchitecture, reflected by relatively high accuracy and few incorrect predictions.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the results of Tutorial 3.

claim: The predictive accuracy of functional networks by cytoarchitecture was similar when excluding vertices within approximately 6 mm of the network boundaries.
source: The predictive accuracy did not appear to be negatively impacted by minor misalignments of the atlas, as the predictive accuracy was similar when excluding vertices within approximately 6 mm of the network boundaries (accuracy mean ± SD [%], original = 12.4 ± 15.4, excluding boundaries = 12.1 ± 13.3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the results of Tutorial 3.

claim: The singular nature of BigBrain currently prohibits replication and does not capture important inter-individual variation.
source: Despite all its promises, the singular nature of BigBrain currently prohibits replication and does not capture important inter-individual variation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text discussing limitations of BigBrain.

claim: Large-scale cytoarchitectural patterns are conserved across individuals, but the position of areal boundaries relative to sulci vary, especially in association cortex.
source: While large-scale cytoarchitectural patterns are conserved across individuals, the position of areal boundaries relative to sulci vary, especially in association cortex (Amunts et al., 2020; Fischl et al., 2008; Zilles and Amunts, 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Amunts et al., 2020, Fischl et al., 2008, and Zilles and Amunts, 2013.

claim: Low predictive accuracy of functional communities by cytoarchitecture may be attributable to subject-specific topographies.
source: For instance, in tutorial 3, low predictive accuracy of functional communities by cytoarchitecture may be attributable to the subject-specific topographies, which are well established in functional imaging (Benkarim et al., 2020; Braga and Buckner, 2017; Gordon et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Benkarim et al., 2020, Braga and Buckner, 2017, Gordon et al., 2017, and Kong et al., 2019.

claim: The BigBrain team is working on new histology-based 3D models in the context of the HIBALL project.
